title: LUA analyzer review — findings ledger, wave 1
why: M60's lang-completion-matrix records lua at 1 pass / 1 disclosed / 7 n-a-or-fail against java's 8-of-9 and done:true. This ledger records what wave 1 MEASURED. Every row names the instrument that produced it and whether the claim is PROVEN (an instrument ran and showed it) or SUSPECTED (read in source, not yet reproduced). Nothing here is a fix; a defect class earns a permanent gate before its fix counts (IDE Honesty Contract §11.1, the F7 rule).

method.productionPath: src/ast/pool-worker parseFile — the same path the indexer uses, so every number here is what the store would receive
method.control: luvit@199 files, 0 parse errors, 0 crashes. A lane needs a set known to be good as well as sets that find defects, or every finding is a maybe.

findings.status: PROVEN
findings.title: Every lua relationship reaches the store with no line number
findings.detail: RealLuaAnalyzer.addRelationship (src/ast/real-lua-analyzer.ts:314-320) constructs {source, target, type, confidence, metadata} and nothing else. There is no line_number, no line, no position. Proven on a purpose-built probe: 15 of 15 relationships carried zero line fields, while the java analyzer through the SAME parseFile path emits line_number:2 on its calls edge. The M60 `lines` column for lua reads n/a; this is why.
findings.whyItMatters: M59.A7/M60 make a stored line a first-class fact. An edge that cannot name its site cannot be checked by a human, and per-site edges are impossible while this holds.

compoundingDefect.title: Site information is destroyed by the dedup key
compoundingDefect.detail: addRelationship dedupes on `type\u001f source \u001f target` (line 316). N distinct call sites for the same callee collapse into ONE edge, so even once line_number is added the first-wins/last-wins choice silently discards every other site. Java carries per-site edges; lua cannot.
compoundingDefect.status: PROVEN by code reading of the dedup key; a reproducing probe is owed.

findings.status: FIXED — gate 11/11, 4/4 mutants
findings.title: coroutineUsage is structurally always 0
findings.detail: countCoroutineSymbols (line 454-458) counts symbols whose metadata.isCoroutine is true. NO code path anywhere in the analyzer ever sets isCoroutine. processCall adds the string 'Coroutines' to ctx.patterns (line 232-234) and stops. findings.status: PROVEN
findings.title: The analyzer's entire metadata block is dropped at the worker boundary
findings.detail: RealLuaAnalyzer returns a rich metadata object (complexity, cyclomaticComplexity, framework, patterns, detectedFrameworks, frameworkPatterns, architecturalInsights, architecturalScore, codeQuality, hasTypeInference, hasFrameworkIntelligence, performanceScore, memoryEfficiency, coroutineUsage, analysisVersion — lines 80-100). The pool-worker symbol mapper (src/ast/pool-worker.ts:549-590) carries a deliberately narrow allowlist and, by its own comment, dropped the whole metadata object; only isDeclaration is carried. A probe through production parseFile returned metadata keys EMPTY, and performanceScore / memoryEfficiency / detectedFrameworks / architecturalScore / codeQuality all came back undefined.
findings.scopeCaveat: This is a PIPELINE characteristic, not lua-specific — java's metadata is also absent through the same path. It is recorded on the lua lane because these specific metadata fields are ones the lua analyzer computes and nobody receives. Whether the fix belongs in lua, in the pipeline, or in both is OPEN and is a decision, not a defect to be silently patched.

findings.status: FIXED — gate 11/11 both directions
findings.title: Framework detection fires on bare identifiers, so an ordinary variable names a framework
findings.detail: detectFrameworks (line 410-419) is called on EVERY identifier node (processNode case 'identifier', line 121-123) and matches bare text: `use`, `setup`, `GetTime`, `C_Timer`, `Proto`, `UIParent`. A probe declaring `local setup = 1; local use = 2` therefore marks an ordinary file as Neovim Configuration. This is a name-equality heuristic, not an AST-derived fact — the analyzer's own header (line 2-3) claims 'Declarations and relationships come from Tree-sitter nodes/fields. No regex fallback or source-wide scanning is used.' A bare-name match on an identifier node is source-wide scanning wearing an AST costume.
findings.resolution: A framework is claimed only from a QUALIFIED member access (vim./love./ngx./resty./display./system./transition./Runtime./lovr./redis) or from a required module name. A bare identifier never names a framework. The gate asserts BOTH directions: a file with variables named use/setup/GetTime claims no framework, AND a file really using vim.api is still labelled Neovim — so the fix cannot be satisfied by deleting detection. Measured: the probe that was labelled both 'Neovim Configuration' and 'World of Warcraft Addon' now claims neither.

findings.status: RETRACTED — THE FINDING WAS WRONG
findings.title: RETRACTED: 'lua symbol positions do not survive the worker boundary'
findings.originalClaim: Every lua symbol reported startLine undefined through production parseFile, while java reported startLine:2 — so lua's range object is not in the shape the mapper expects.
findings.whatMeasurementActuallyShows: Positions are correct and complete. A raw dump of every own key on every symbol for `local plainvar = 1 / local multi1, multi2 = 2, 3 / local returned = "exported"` gives plainvar@1, multi1@2, multi2@2, returned@3, each with correct endLine, startIndex and endIndex. Symbols are fine.
findings.whyTheProbeWasWrong: The probe read `s.range?.startLine`. The pool-worker mapper does not carry a `range` object at all — it flattens the analyzer's range into top-level `startLine` / `endLine` / `startIndex` / `endIndex` (src/ast/pool-worker.ts:553-556). So `s.range` is undefined for EVERY language, and my probe read a field that the pipeline deliberately does not emit. Java looked correct in the same probe only because I read `startLine` there.
findings.theLesson: This is the second time in this wave that a probe's own field access, not the code under test, produced the finding. The first was the gate's attributor. The tell in both cases is the same: a finding that says a value is MISSING when the pipeline's contract says the value lives somewhere else. Before claiming a position defect, read the mapper.
findings.gate: n/a — nothing to gate; the symbols were never broken

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED
findings.title: setmetatable / constructor detection is order-dependent
findings.detail: constructorTarget (line 287-293) admits a `.new`/`:new`/`.constructor` call only if ctx.declaredTables ALREADY has the table, and declaredTables is filled during the same single traversal. The setmetatable branch (line 235-247) is likewise unguarded on ordering for the reverse case. A use-before-declaration therefore loses an edge that a declare-before-use file keeps — the same source semantics, two different graphs. A probe put setmetatable(Account, AccountMeta) BEFORE the declarations; the extends edge did survive, so the guarded path (setmetatable) is not obviously order-sensitive, but the `.new` path is untested and is the one the guard actually wraps.
findings.gate: covered by the lua truth oracle, whose `ctor` rule is also order-independent by construction
findings.adjudication: Reproduced with two files differing only in statement order. `local A = {} / function A.new() end / A.new()` emitted `instantiates global->A`; `A.new() / local A = {} / function A.new() end` emitted NOTHING. Same semantics, different graph — so the edge was a fact about the traversal, not about the program.
findings.fix: collectDeclaredTables runs as a PRE-PASS before the walk, so a constructor call no longer depends on where its table was declared. Both orders now emit the edge, each at its own call's line (L3 and L1 respectively).

findings.status: RETRACTED as stated
findings.title: Two same-named locals in different functions become one identity
findings.detail: Symbol identity is the bare name. addContainsRelationships (line 305-312) keys Contains edges on owner||scope name only. A `local item` inside f() and a `local item` inside g() both produce owner f/g, so the edges stay apart, but any consumer keying on (name, scope) still collides across files and the store's symbol identity contract (a member's identity is its container, not its bare name — the M49 W2 ruling) is not honoured for lua locals.
findings.adjudication: Measured directly: two locals both named `item`, one in f() and one in g(), produce DISTINCT symbols (`owner=f@L2`, `owner=g@L6`) and DISTINCT contains edges (`f->item@L2`, `g->g@L6`). The claim that same-named locals in different functions collapse into one identity is FALSE. The residual question — two same-named locals in the SAME function — was not measured and is not claimed.

findings.status: RETRACTED — not reachable
findings.title: An unnamed function can be named after its own parameter list
findings.detail: extractFunction (line 130) falls back to node.namedChild(0) when the `name` field is absent. For a nameless function that first named child is the `parameters` node, so the symbol's name would become the parameter list's source text. Comment on line 132 says anonymous functions are skipped, but the guard tests the RESULTING name for emptiness, not the node's shape.
findings.gate: PENDING — a reproducing probe is owed
findings.adjudication: Measured: no symbol is ever named after a parameter list or a source snippet. `local anon = function(a,b) ... end` yields only the variable `anon`, and a nameless function as a table field yields only the table variable. The reason is structural: processNode's switch has no case for `function_definition`, so an anonymous function is never dispatched at all and the `|| namedChild(0)` name fallback in extractFunction is never reached for one. The fallback is a latent hazard, not a live defect.

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED (LUA-09). The `return {}` half is the real half; `return require(...)` is recorded as deliberately open below.
findings.title: extractExport handled `return <name>` and nothing else — the dominant module shape published nothing
findings.detail: extractExport required target.type === 'identifier', so a returned table literal — the standard Lua module surface — published no export at all. The `return M` idiom was covered, which is why the 2-file fixture differential never noticed it. Sized by grammar-based census of the two pinned corpora (script/m60/lua-export-census.ts, counted off the wired wasm, not a regex): 366 of Kong's 1,309 files and 33 of Luvit's 199 carried 1,377 nameable exports, all lost.
findings.gate: script/m60/verify-lua-export-shapes.ts — 24 checks, 5/5 planted mutations caught, and every planted mutant is reverted with the analyzer restored byte-for-byte. Committed as a fixture too: validation/m14/fixtures/lua/export-shapes.lua + .expectation.json, which also pins the export LINE of every member (M59) and forbids three fabrications.
findings.adjudication: The first corpus run reported ONE spurious export on luvit and ONE on kong, and in BOTH cases the ANALYZER was right and the CENSUS was too narrow. luvit/deps/tls/lcrypto.lua returns from inside a terminal if/else (lines 42-46 of 46) and the census only looked at chunk's direct children. kong/kong/init.lua returns `init` from inside a file-scope `do` block opened at line 36, and the wired grammar builds that as `chunk > do_statement > block > …` — two levels down — which the first walker did not descend. Two rounds of the instrument blaming correct code, which is the failure mode this lane exists to catch; both were fixed in the census, not by weakening the analyzer. A third round came from the gate itself, which asserted a loop-body return was NOT a module export; Lua's `return` exits the chunk, so it is, and the gate was corrected to the analyzer's rule.
findings.fix: src/ast/real-lua-analyzer.ts extractExport now publishes the members a returned table_constructor NAMES, and nothing else. The `name` FIELD is read, never a namedChild(0) fallback: for a positional entry that fallback yields the VALUE, and a `return { "a", "b" }` would have published exports named after the module's own array elements. Measured node shapes: `a = 1` puts an identifier in the field; `["k"] = 1` puts a STRING there with the unquoted text under `content`; a positional entry has no name field at all.
findings.rule: A return reachable WITHOUT ENTERING A FUNCTION is a possible module surface, and the module publishes the UNION of what every such return can name. The boundary is the FUNCTION, not the block structure — so a return inside a terminal if/else, a file-scope `do` block, or a loop body all count, and a return inside a function does not. This is stricter than 'the last return wins' and it is what makes the corpus agree exactly.
findings.evidence: Direct-path corpus check (parseWithAnalyzer, because parseFile discards exports at the worker boundary and would report 0 for a perfect analyzer): luvit recall 1.0000 (186/186) precision 1.0000; kong recall 1.0000 (1,579/1,579) precision 1.0000, 0 spurious. Expected names come from an independent grammar walk, so the two sides are separate derivations of the same question.
findings.residual: Deliberately NOT published, and pinned silent so a future change cannot start inventing them unnoticed: `return require("x")` (a re-export — naming it means inventing an export name from a module path, which is a different relationship), `return "literal"` (17 kong files), and `return setmetatable(M, mt)` (5 kong files, where the exported table is the first argument). Real surfaces, not named. Open, not guessed at.

findings.status: FIXED
findings.title: A published score rewards a pattern the analyzer never detects
findings.detail: calculateArchitecturalScore (line 460-467) grants +5 when ctx.patterns has 'Module/Table Pattern'. No code path ever adds that string — the patterns actually added are 'Object-Oriented Programming', 'Object-Oriented Programming (Metatables)', 'Object-Oriented Programming (Libraries)' and 'Coroutines'. So the score is computed from a dead branch, and codeQuality (line 469-475) inherits the error because it thresholds on that score.

findings.status: FIXED
findings.title: performanceScore and memoryEfficiency are constants published as measurements
findings.detail: Lines 96-97 return the literals 85 and 85. No measurement produces them. Per Truth Rule 1 a fact a reader cannot check is not a fact; these are the two most checkable-looking numbers in the block and they are the two that are invented.

findings.status: PROVEN - found while fixing LUA-01
findings.title: A call split across two lines is deleted from the graph entirely
findings.detail: processCall took the callee's name from node.text. For a call written as `obj\n  .method()` that text is a multi-line SOURCE SNIPPET, not a name. The pool-worker's garbage-target filter (src/ast/pool-worker.ts:391) rejects any relationship target containing a newline, so the edge was dropped. Measured: `obj.method()` on one line produced the edge `caller2 -> obj.method`; the byte-identical call split across two lines produced NO EDGE AT ALL. Line breaks are ordinary in real Lua, so this silently deletes calls from the graph.
findings.whyItMatters: Not merely an ugly name: a missing edge is a missing relationship a user cannot see is missing.
findings.fix: The callee's name and the node carrying its line are now read together from structure (callee()): for `table . field` / `table : field` the callee is `field`, the LAST named child, and its own start position is the line the method name is written on. Name and line cannot drift apart because they are the same node.
findings.gate: script/m60/verify-lua-edge-lines.ts - the multi-line fixture is the falsifier; a whole-line implementation passes every other row and fails it

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED
findings.title: An anonymous function established no scope, so a closure's internal `return` was published as the FILE's export
findings.detail: The walk created a frame only for `function_declaration`. A `function_definition` — an anonymous function, a closure — shared its enclosing frame entirely. Two measured symptoms: (1) extractExport's guard was `if (frame.callable) return`, so a closure at FILE scope had no callable and its internal `return x` was published as the file's export — reproduced: `local t = { cb = function(x) return x end }` plus `return { a = 1 }` published an export named "x" from inside the closure while the file's real return published nothing; (2) a closure's own locals were attributed to the enclosing named function — `local captured` inside a closure nested in `outer` came out with ownerName "outer".
findings.whyItMattered: Closures are ubiquitous in Lua — every callback is one. A file whose only `return` was inside a callback published that callback's return as the module's public API.
findings.fix: LuaFrame carries `inFunction`, set on entering ANY function body including a nameless closure, and extractExport's guard tests that. The guard could not be fixed by giving a nameless closure a synthetic callable: that would fabricate a symbol to solve a scoping problem, and a synthetic identity is worse than the bug. A nameless closure keeps the enclosing callable as its label and gets its own localNames.
findings.gate: script/m60/verify-lua-member-identity.ts — 17/17 checks, 6/6 mutants, including an ANTI-VACUITY leg: the fixture ends with a real `return use` and the gate asserts it IS published, so "no closure return leaked" cannot pass on an empty set

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED
findings.title: A closure's frame did not inherit the enclosing scope's locals, so an UPVALUE assignment was published as a new declaration
findings.detail: The frame created on entering a function body held only that function's parameters. A closure can SEE the enclosing scope's locals — that is what a closure is — so an assignment to a captured variable looked like a fresh declaration. Measured at luvit/deps/utils.lua:99: inside `function (e, ...)` nested in `local function adapt(c, fn, ...)`, the statement `c = nil` emitted `contains adapt -> c` — a containment edge naming `c`, which HAS NO SYMBOL, because `c` is a parameter of adapt and parameters are not emitted as symbols. The result was an edge pointing at nothing.
findings.fix: The frame created on entering a function now starts from a COPY of the enclosing frame's localNames and adds its own parameters. Inheriting is also simply what the language says: the assignment mutates adapt's parameter, it does not declare anything.
findings.gate: covered by the lua truth oracle plus verify-lua-member-identity; the observable was a containment edge naming a symbol that does not exist

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED
findings.title: A call through a computed index published its EXPRESSION as the relationship target
findings.detail: callee() fell through to `functionNode.text` for any callee that was not a plain identifier or a dot/method index. `dao[method or context .. "_by_" .. endpoint_key](dao, ...)` — kong/api/endpoints.lua:260 — therefore produced a `calls` edge whose target was the whole 48-character expression. That is a payload masquerading as a name: unmatchable to any declaration, unreferenceable, and unbounded in shape. It is the defect class M60 records for other lanes ('publishes the target "ns.Iface<number>", a payload rather than a name').
findings.fix: A bracket_index_expression callee is skipped. A LITERAL index (`dao["rows"]`) is a name and still handled. Skipped rather than guessed: a computed callee is not a fact about the call graph, and inventing a name for it is the same fabrication under another spelling.
findings.the_gate_caught_my_own_repeat_of_LUA_00: The first version of the fix tested for `table_index_expression`, which is what the 0.5.0 grammar repo's node-types.json calls it. The WIRED grammar emits `bracket_index_expression` — measured by parsing `dao[expr](x)`. So the branch was unreachable and the fix would have done nothing, silently. verify-lua-grasped-fields reported `node type "table_index_expression" is never emitted by the grammar` and the gate built for exactly that defect class caught it, in the same lane, on the same mistake. That is the third time this instrument has caught a real gap in itself (the other two were anonymous functions and the same computed index), and the second time it caught ME.
findings.note_on_the_oracle: The truth oracle had the SAME defect — it emitted a truth edge for a computed-index callee — so the two sides agreed on a wrong answer and the differential could not see it. An oracle that shares a defect is worse than no oracle, because it launders the defect into agreement. Both sides now skip it, and that is the point of recording it.

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED — found by the lane's own new fixture lane, on its first run
findings.title: A bare `local x` with NO assignment produced no symbol and no containment edge
findings.detail: A variable_declaration has TWO shapes, measured: `local a, b = 1, 2` is variable_declaration > assignment_statement > variable_list + expression_list, while `local solo` is variable_declaration > variable_list with NO assignment_statement at all. The LUA-00 fix read namedChild(0) as the assignment and then looked for a variable_list INSIDE it, so the second shape returned nothing. The declaration was silently dropped.
findings.whyItSurvivedLUA00: It was ALREADY broken before LUA-00 — the pre-fix `childForFieldName('name_list') || namedChild(0)` landed on the identifier, whose namedChildCount is 0, so the loop never ran. It survived that fix because the corpus measurement was byte-identical across the change (3,610 symbols before and after), so the fix was invisible to the only instrument being run, and nothing asserted the SHAPE. A 1,510-file corpus cannot see a shape that no corpus file happens to exercise in a way that changes a count.
findings.howItWasFound: The committed M14.0.F3 fixture lane, on its first run, in a fixture written to pin LUA-00's OBSERVABLE consequence. A fixture asserting 'the plainest declarations in the language are extracted' failed on the plainest declaration there is.
findings.fix: The lookup distinguishes the two shapes: namedChild(0) is the assignment only when it IS an assignment_statement, and the variable_list is taken directly otherwise. The value is likewise absent for the bare form, so the isTable test has nothing to test.

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED — and the ORACLE was wrong, not the census
findings.title: The oracle derived 218 export edges the census did not, because it never framed an ANONYMOUS function
findings.detail: After LUA-09 the oracle's truth side read 1,797 export edges against the census's 1,579 on the same kong corpus. The oracle's count was the LARGER of the two, which is the wrong way round — the oracle dedupes (label, from, target) globally while the census sums a per-file set, so the oracle's distinct count should be the smaller. That arithmetic alone says the oracle over-derives. script/m60/lua-export-truth-diff.ts settled it: census-only names were ZERO, so the census is a strict subset and every one of the 218 came from the oracle.
findings.likelyCause: The oracle's walk carries a `scope` string and pushes/pops a frame on function boundaries; the census's walk skips `function_definition` and `function_declaration` node types outright. If the oracle does not frame some function FORM — a function assigned in a table field, or a `function M:f()` method — then a return inside it is attributed to global scope and becomes a spurious `exports global -> …` truth edge. That is a hypothesis from the shape of the two implementations, NOT a measurement: it has not been tested.
findings.whyItMatters: The oracle's observed side for exports is 0 (LUA-14, exports are discarded at the worker boundary), so the export comparison is currently VACUOUS on the observed side and this disagreement is invisible in it. When LUA-14 is fixed, a truth set that is 218 edges too large would surface as 218 unexplained edges and be indistinguishable from a real analyzer defect.
findings.whatWouldSettleIt: Extract the two name sets and diff them. Any name the oracle derives and the census does not names a file, and that file's return is the one to read. This is a few lines against the two artifacts and was not run because the LUA-09 fix and its gate came first.
findings.notClaimed: The analyzer-side result never depended on either walker: the census and the analyzer are independent derivations and agreed exactly (recall 1.0000, precision 1.0000, 0 spurious on both corpora). This finding was about the two TRUTH walkers, and it is now closed by fixing the oracle.
findings.gate: script/m60/lua-export-truth-diff.ts — compares the two walkers' name sets per file, exits non-zero on any disagreement, and carries a selftest that re-runs the oracle's export rule with the fnDepth guard REMOVED: 820 identifier returns reappear from inside anonymous functions on a 400-file slice. A diff that cannot fail is a diff that cannot have been what found this.
findings.rootCause: lua-truth-oracle.ts walk(): `const childScope = node.type === 'function_declaration' || node.type === 'function_definition' ? (functionNameOf(node)?.label ?? scope) : scope`. functionNameOf returns null when the node has no `name` field — which is EXACTLY the anonymous `function_definition` — so the `?? scope` fallback means an anonymous function opens NO scope, and its body is walked as if it were file scope. Every `return` inside one therefore satisfied the export rule. Read on kong/kong/pdk/service/response.lua: L69 `return response_headers, err` sits 4 spaces deep inside `attach_resp_headers_mt = function(response_headers, err)` (a table FIELD holding an anonymous function, L61) and L113 `return v` sits inside `__index = function(_, name)` (L84). The oracle derived `exports global -> response_headers` and `exports global -> v`; the analyzer published neither, correctly.
findings.classOfDefect: This is LUA-20 in the INSTRUMENT. LUA-20 was an anonymous function sharing its enclosing frame so that its internal return was published as the FILE's export; it was found and fixed in the analyzer, and the same shape was never fixed in the oracle that checks the analyzer. It stayed invisible until LUA-09 made exports measurable at all — before that the oracle's export rule only fired on `return <ident>`, and no corpus file combined an anonymous function with a file-scope-looking return often enough to surface it. A defect can be absent from the evidence because the evidence never asked.
findings.fix: The walk now carries `fnDepth`, incremented on entering ANY function_declaration or function_definition, and the export rule requires `fnDepth === 0` in addition to `scope === 'global'`. Depth, deliberately, not a synthetic scope name: naming an anonymous function `<anon@L113>` would fix exports AND silently change every contains/calls edge inside it, because those carry the scope as their source. Depth answers only the question the export rule asks. Verified: calls, contains, extends, instantiates and imports are byte-identical before and after (26,408 / 29,726 / 103 / 10 / 3,523), and export truth moved 1,797 -> 1,579.
findings.result: kong: 0 files disagree, 1,579 = 1,579, 813 global distinct on both sides. luvit: 0 files disagree, 186 = 186, 138 distinct on both sides.

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED — the ORACLE was wrong, not the analyzer
findings.title: The oracle never registered file-scope locals, so every upvalue write looked like a new declaration
findings.detail: lua-truth-oracle.ts walked `if (scope !== 'global')` before writing to `localsIn`, while pushing the `contains` edge unconditionally. So `local prev_min_at` at kong/cluster_events/init.lua:272 produced a contains edge but left `localsIn.get('global')` empty. `visibleInChain` then walked `poll` -> `global`, found nothing, returned false, and the oracle demanded `contains poll -> prev_min_at` for the upvalue WRITE at :286. The analyzer does not emit it and is right: prev_min_at is a file-scope local that poll closes over, not a local of poll.
findings.classOfDefect: LUA-21's shape again, in the instrument. LUA-21 was an upvalue assignment emitting a containment edge naming a symbol that does not exist; it was fixed in the analyzer, and the oracle's ORA-4 guard for the same case was blind to file scope the whole time.
findings.fix: Removed the `scope !== 'global'` guard so file-scope locals are registered like every other. 242 of kong's 290 analyzer-attributable missing edges were this one missing line; contains recall 0.9872 -> 0.9952.
findings.gate: The residue is visible in every oracle run's three-way split, which is now reported as analyzer / noise-filter / pipeline-discarded rather than lumped together.
findings.notClaimed: The ~80 analyzer-attributable figure this lane carried was wrong. With a three-way split the true figure was 290, and 289 of those were oracle over-derivation.

findings.status: OPEN — and now MEASURED, so the decision needs no further argument. Owner call.
findings.title: Should a for-loop's control variable be a symbol? The oracle said yes for 2,921 edges, then the answer was withdrawn
findings.detail: An earlier version of this oracle DID derive `contains scope -> <loop var>` for for_numeric_clause and for_generic_clause. That produced 2,921 extra missing edges on kong and read as 2,921 analyzer defects. It was not: a two-function probe shows the analyzer emits `sel2 -> listener` and NOT `sel -> listener` for two loops that differ only in whether the body ASSIGNS the variable. The analyzer has no for-clause declaration rule at all — for_statement appears in it once, as a complexity counter — so that symbol is manufactured by the assignment, not the loop.
findings.bothPositions: FOR: a for-loop variable is a local binding in Lua, so `contains sel -> listener` is a true statement. AGAINST: its scope is the LOOP, not the function, so filing it under the function is imprecise, and a binding that lives one iteration is rarely a navigation target.
findings.whyNotDecided: This is a question about what the symbol table MEANS, and the oracle is not entitled to answer it by deriving edges the analyzer never claimed. Deriving them converted an open design question into 2,921 apparent defects, which is the worst possible failure mode for an instrument.
findings.alsoExplains: The run's single UNEXPLAINED edge, `contains Schema:errors_to_string -> err` at kong/db/schema/init.lua. `err` is bound by no local — it is bound by `for _, err in pairs(...)` at :2307 and ASSIGNED at :2320. The assignment is what makes the analyzer emit the edge. The oracle is silent on the loop, so the two agree by coincidence rather than by derivation, which is why the edge surfaced as unexplained. Two routes to one true edge.
findings.ownerDecision: Whether loop variables belong in the symbol graph. Until then the oracle derives neither, and the coincidence above is documented so it is not read as a defect.

blastRadius.corpus: 400 of kong's 1,309 files, measured through the direct analyzer path
blastRadius.topNames: _ 359, v 142, k 102, i 96, name 38, field 33, key 29, plugin 25, err 24 — the top four are 52% of all bindings

theDecidingFacts: The cost is asymmetric: +2.0% symbols but +12.1% contains edges, because each binding is an edge and most names are reused.
More than half the bindings are four single characters. `contains global -> v` is a true statement and it is navigation noise; the two are not the same thing.
A quarter of all bindings are `_`, which by Lua convention means discard — a real binding, and the least useful symbol in any language that has one.

The scope is wrong by construction. A loop variable is live in the LOOP BODY, not in the function, so `contains fn -> v` asserts a membership that outlives the binding. The honest model is a scope this analyzer does not have, because a `for` clause opens none.
findings.recommendation: Keep the current answer — loop variables are NOT symbols — on the evidence rather than on principle, and record it as a DECISION rather than a gap. The +12.1% edge growth buys 240 names of which the top four are single letters, and it files a loop-body binding as a member of the enclosing function, which is a false membership claim. The single edge that depends on the opposite answer is the LUA-26 coincidence, exempted structurally in the oracle rather than resolved by deriving an edge the oracle deliberately refuses to derive.
findings.whatWouldChangeThis: A consumer that navigates by containment and would benefit, or a decision to model the `for` clause as opening a scope — which is the real fix and a larger change. If loop variables are wanted they should be symbols in a LOOP scope, not members of the function; the frame model has no such scope, so the cheap version of this is the wrong shape.

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED — a guard copied from another file, never re-measured, dead for LUA-22's whole life
findings.title: The oracle's computed-index guard tested for a node type the grammar never emits
findings.detail: calleeOf tested `n.type === 'table_index_expression'`. The wired grammar emits `bracket_index_expression` — the ANALYZER's own LUA-22 fix had already corrected the name, with a comment recording that `table_index_expression` was what the 0.5.0 grammar repo's node-types.json calls it. The oracle's copy kept the wrong name, so the guard never fired and every computed-index call fell through to `return { name: n.text }`. 46 truth targets on kong were whole programs: `dao[method or context .. "_by_" .. endpoint_key]`.
findings.fix: Corrected to `bracket_index_expression`, and the whole no-name class is now a WHITELIST (identifier / dot / method / bracket) rather than a growing blacklist — because two blacklists in a row is how this happened: each named a type somebody had to measure, and the type nobody re-measured stayed wrong forever.
findings.lesson: A guard copied into a second file and never re-measured against the grammar is how a fixed defect stays fixed on one side and live on the other.

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED — the ORACLE was deriving incoherent edges
findings.title: The oracle demanded `contains new_router -> new_router`: a scope as a member of itself
findings.detail: Five such edges on kong (new_router L426, initialize L36, sleep_once_for_balancer_init L802 and two more), each filed as an analyzer miss. `contains X -> X` is incoherent on any reading — the scope IS the name — and the analyzer's member-identity gate has a standing check that no symbol duplicates its own owner. findings.fix: Skipped at both contains derivations (`local-decl` and `assign-decl`) and COUNTED, reported in the run as `selfContainmentSkipped`, so the skip is visible rather than silent.
findings.why: A skip that is not reported is indistinguishable from a bug in the skip. Five edges that vanished without a number would have looked like the oracle quietly losing coverage.

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED — a REAL ANALYZER DEFECT, exposed only after the oracle stopped sharing it
findings.title: A call on a call published the whole inner call as the relationship target
findings.detail: callee() fell through to `functionNode.text` for any callee it had no branch for, so `require("some.module")()` produced the target `require("some.module")` — a payload, not a name, the same defect class LUA-22 fixed for computed indexes two lines above. This is the argument the LUA-22 comment makes about an oracle that shares a defect — demonstrated rather than asserted. Fixing the oracle's side first is what exposed it.
findings.fix: A WHITELIST of the four name-bearing callee forms, for LUA-27's reason.
findings.gate: script/m60/verify-lua-call-targets.ts — 25 checks, including an F7 mutation leg that deletes the whitelist from callee() and requires the gate to go RED, with the analyzer restored byte-for-byte. findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED — found by the LUA-29 gate, and documented in a comment that was lying
findings.title: A literal string index is a name, and LUA-22's fix threw it away with the computed ones
findings.detail: `dao["rows"]()` names exactly the field `dao.rows()` names, but the measured tree builds both as `bracket_index_expression` — the literal one as {table, field=string}, the computed one as {table, field=<expr>} — so LUA-22's type-level branch could not tell them apart and dropped the whole class. Measured on a probe: `dao["rows"]()` produced NO EDGE while `dao.rows()` produced calls:rows.
findings.theLieInTheComment: The LUA-22 comment stated "a literal index (`dao[\"rows\"]`) IS a name and is handled by the dot/method branch above". That was false: a literal index is a bracket_index_expression, never a dot or method one, so the intent was documented and never implemented. A comment asserting a behaviour is not evidence that the behaviour exists — and this lane has now been bitten by a comment twice (here, and by the reachability gate attributing a field literal to the wrong node).
findings.fix: Only a literal STRING names a field, on both sides, from the measured `field` child: string -> the unquoted content; number -> an array index, not a name; identifier -> a VARIABLE holding the key, not statically knowable.
findings.independentlyReached: The analyzer and the oracle were changed from the grammar measurement, separately, and reached the same rule. That is the only kind of agreement worth having — not one side copied from the other.

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED — the classifier was EXCUSING edges by inferring, and a collapsed analyzer passed clean
findings.title: A label the pipeline emitted zero times was called 'structurally undeliverable' — so a broken analyzer read as a perfect one
findings.detail: The three-way split added for LUA-14 excused a missing edge whenever its label had not been seen anywhere in the pipeline output. That inference fails in the one direction that matters most: if the analyzer emits NOTHING for a label, the pipeline also emits nothing, the label looks discarded, and every truth edge for it is excused. A collapsed analyzer and a dropped field become indistinguishable.
findings.caughtBy: Mutation, not reading. Neutering addContainsRelationships — dropping EVERY synthesized contains edge — moved kong's missing from 3 to 47 on a 5-file slice and STILL reported `analyzer=0`, with all 47 filed as pipeline-discarded. The differential passed a totally broken analyzer. That is the exact failure this lane exists to prevent, committed by the very fix that was meant to improve the split, and it was only visible because the corpus mutation harness was built.
findings.fix: The verdict must be evidence. The oracle now parses the same file through BOTH paths (parseFile and parseWithAnalyzer, capped at 150 files and the cap reported) and calls a label discarded only where the direct path supplied it and the pipeline did not, on that same file. Absence on both sides proves nothing. After the fix, M8 moves the reading from `analyzer=0` to `analyzer=648`.
findings.secondBlindSpotFound: Exports were compared only through parseFile, which discards the field (LUA-14) — so the export comparison was a comparison against an empty set. Not a weak signal but NO signal: a mutation deleting the entire returned-table export branch (LUA-09) or republishing every in-function return (LUA-20) left the pipeline output byte-identical, and BOTH SURVIVED. The oracle now compares exports on the direct path against the same tree-derived truth, and both are caught (missed 0->14, spurious 0->42).
findings.duplicationRemoved: That direct-path export measurement already existed as script/m60/lua-export-census.ts. Having it in two places is what let them drift into the 218-edge phantom disagreement of LUA-24. One instrument, two paths, one truth.

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED — a REAL ANALYZER DEFECT, invisible through the pipeline and found by a seam probe
findings.title: `setmetatable(X, { ... })` published the whole table constructor as the extends TARGET
findings.detail: The setmetatable branch guarded only its FIRST argument with `!isTableNode(target)` and then used `metatable.text` as the relationship target. So `setmetatable(self, { __index = super })` published `extends self -> { __index = super }` — a payload, not a name. Two measured losses on kong: `self -> { __index = super }` at kong/db/dao/init.lua:990 and `_M -> { __call = ..., __index = ... }` at kong/cmd/utils/log.lua:88, the latter spanning five lines.
findings.whyItWasInvisible: That target contains NEWLINES, and pool-worker rejects any relationship target containing one — so the edge never reached the store. Through the pipeline the defect was not measurable: the edge was simply ABSENT, indistinguishable from an edge that was never derived, and the oracle's byLabel figures showed extends at 103/103 with zero missing and zero unexplained. LUA-29's whitelist fixed the same defect class on the `callee()` path and never touched this one.
findings.howItSurfaced: The direct-vs-pipeline seam probe added for LUA-31 compares the two paths per file and reports labels the pipeline drops. It flagged `extends` alongside `exports` as proven-discarded, which is what pointed at the two files. A defect the pipeline filters out can only be found by a path the pipeline does not filter.
findings.fix: A single shared `nameBearing()` rule — identifier, dot_index, method_index — used by BOTH the callee whitelist and the setmetatable path, so the two cannot drift apart the way `table_index_expression` did (LUA-27). `setmetatable(A, M)` still yields `A->M`; an inline or computed metatable yields nothing, because there is no name for it.
findings.gate: script/m60/verify-lua-call-targets.ts, extended to 29 checks, with the LUA-32 cases proven red by reverting the fix (4 failures, each showing the exact payload target) and the source restored byte-for-byte.

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED — the ORACLE, again, and again as the mirror of the fix that corrected it
findings.title: The oracle's setmetatable rule relaxed a type requirement into no requirement at all
findings.detail: LUA-18 retracted an `extends` over-fabrication claim: the oracle required `meta.type === 'identifier'`, called 3 genuine edges fabrications, and recorded analyzer precision as 0.7. The correction was right about member expressions (`Emitter.meta`) and wrong about everything else — dropping the type requirement entirely let `setmetatable(_G, nil)` derive `extends _G -> nil` (5 kong sites), `setmetatable(opts or {}, defaults)` derive a SOURCE that is a binary expression, and `setmetatable(env.ngx, getmetatable(ngx))` derive a call as a target. 16 edges, all the oracle's, all correctly refused by the analyzer after LUA-32.
findings.fix: The LUA-32 rule, which the analyzer adopted in the same pass and this rule missed: an endpoint must be a NAME. identifier / dot_index_expression / method_index_expression carry one; nil, a call, a binary expression and a table constructor do not. `nil` is not a superclass and `getmetatable(ngx)` is not a name. Both sides now share one `nameBearing()` rule, so they cannot drift the way `table_index_expression` did (LUA-27).
findings.classOfDefect: A correction applied by REMOVING a constraint rather than by replacing it with the right one. The retraction was correct; the replacement rule was not stated, so the space it left was filled by whatever the code did next — which was nothing.

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED — the LAST structural blind spot in the differential, found by mutation
findings.title: The differential could not see a relationship whose target contained a newline
findings.detail: pool-worker rejects any relationship target containing a NEWLINE. The differential reads relationships through the pipeline, so an edge whose target is a multi-line payload is deleted on the way to the store and is simply ABSENT — indistinguishable from one that was never derived. Measured, not argued: reintroducing the LUA-32 defect (setmetatable publishing a table constructor as the extends target) moved NO number the instrument reported. Missing, unexplained, line accuracy and direct-path exports were all byte-identical, while the mutation provably changed the analyzer's output on 15 of 260 corpus files.
findings.whyItMatters: This is not a hypothetical filter. It is the mechanism by which LUA-32 survived an entire lane of review reading `extends 103/103, zero missing, zero unexplained`, and by which any future payload-target defect will survive the same way. The export half of the same blindness was already found and fixed in LUA-31 — a missing FIELD. This is a missing CONTENT RULE, and it is strictly harder to see because the field is present and populated.
findings.fix: Relationships now get the same two-path treatment exports got: the analyzer's own output against the same tree-derived truth, read through parseWithAnalyzer, with no pipeline filter in between. `spurious` is the leg that matters — a payload target the tree never derived is exactly what a fabricated target is. On kong: 8,346 truth, 8,346 hit, 0 missed, 0 spurious, recall 1.0, precision 1.0 over the 150 probed files.
findings.secondDefectFoundWhileBuildingIt: The leg first reported 317 missed on kong — exactly the export truth count — because exports are a separate array on the direct result and the relationship loop demanded an `exports global -> x` key that the direct relationship list can never contain. The leg was measuring its own blind spot and calling it a recall gap. Fixed by folding the direct exports into the key set, so the relationship leg is complete and the export leg remains a subset view of it.
findings.theOneExemption: LUA-26's coincidence is exempted STRUCTURALLY, not by name: an observed `contains S -> T` is exempt when T is bound by a for-clause in that file, which is how the oracle knows the case exists. A name-based exemption would be a hole shaped exactly like the next bug. Exemptions are counted and reported (`loopCoincidenceExempted`), not silently dropped — a skip with no number looks like lost coverage.

findings.status: PROVEN and FIXED
findings.title: The last silent export shape that carries a NAME, and a disclosure for the ones that do not
findings.detail: LUA-09 left `return require("x")`, `return "literal"` and `return setmetatable(M, mt)` silent. Measured off the wired grammar by script/m60/lua-silent-export-census.ts, at a file's ACTUAL module return: of kong's 1,309 files, 3 carry a setmetatable with a NAME (fixable), 2 a setmetatable with an expression, 3 a re-export, 17 a string literal and 21 another call. luvit: 7 silent files, 0 fixable. A correction to the closure record: it quoted '17 kong files / 5 files' for these shapes, which counted only files where the shape IS the module's primary return; a plain grep at any indent gives 76 and 87, because it also catches returns nested inside functions. Both numbers are right for different questions and the smaller one was quoted without its question.
findings.fix: `return setmetatable(<name>, mt)` publishes the name — the module's surface IS M, exactly as in `return M`, which the analyzer already handled. The metatable is an attribute OF M, not a second export. On kong that is 3 files and +3 exports (1,579 -> 1,582), with recall and precision both 1.0000 on both corpora.
findings.theDisclosure: The other shapes carry NO name and are recorded as `metadata.unpublishedSurface` instead, each entry derived: `shape` from the node type, `detail` from the node's own text, `line` from its start position, `why` a fixed reason per shape. The point is that 'no exports' currently means two indistinguishable things — this module defines nothing, and this module's surface exists but cannot be named — and a disclosure separates them while publishing no name at all. An export called 'kong.tools.dns' for a re-export of kong.tools.dns would be a fabricated name, the same fabrication LUA-22, LUA-29 and LUA-32 refused for relationship targets. The field is ABSENT whenever the surface is nameable, which is the LUA-11 rule: nothing constant-shaped is ever published.
findings.aCallOnACallIsNotAReExport: While wiring this, `return require("x")(-1000)` — 20 kong files — was found to disclose as `call-result` with a null detail, and the analyzer is RIGHT. The outer call's callee is the inner call, which is LUA-29's case: there is no name. An earlier attempt to build the re-export slice by pattern matched those 20 and not the 3 genuine ones, because the pattern cannot see which node the `name` FIELD points at. Found by reading the files, which is the only thing that settles it.
findings.gate: verify-lua-export-shapes, 24 -> 42 checks, F7-proven: removing the block turns it red at 30/6 with the exact missing names printed, and the source is restored byte-for-byte.
findings.thirdDuplication: lua-export-truth-diff.ts had its OWN copy of the census walk. Adding the setmetatable rule to the real census and not the copy produced 3 phantom disagreements — the gate correctly flagging a disagreement that did not exist, and the third time in this lane that one piece of logic in two files has cost real time (LUA-24 was the first, 218 edges). The copy is DELETED: the diff now imports `expectedExportNames` from the census. A differential that re-implements one of its own participants is not a differential, and its disagreement cannot say which side is wrong.
findings.mutation: M14 (the setmetatable arm deleted) and M15 (the disclosure deleted) both caught on real code: exports missed 0 -> 2, disclosures 29 -> 26. The harness is now 14 mutants, all caught, with the no-op control surviving.

rootCause.title: The analyzer asks for five grammar fields that DO NOT EXIST, so five extraction paths never fire
rootCause.thisIsTheHeadline: Every other finding in this ledger is downstream of this one. M14.0.F1 already reports lua's `grammar` cell as status fail for exactly this reason (5 unknown field literals, zero waived), and the LCM matrix carries that fail. It was not acted on because the corpus evidence said 0 parse errors — which is true, and is not the same question.
rootCause.detail: The analyzer requests childForFieldName('name_list') at lines 158 and 183, childForFieldName('function') at line 208, childForFieldName('expression_list') at line 297, and childForFieldName('key') at line 393. The pinned grammar resolves NONE of them on any node. Measured on a probe through the production path, resolving each literal against every named child in the tree: name_list ABSENT, function ABSENT, expression_list ABSENT, key ABSENT, parameters ABSENT, table ABSENT, method ABSENT, field ABSENT. Only name, value and arguments resolve.
rootCause.whatTheGrammarActuallyHas: A `local a, b = 1, 2` is variable_declaration > [anon `local`] > assignment_statement > variable_list [fields: name=identifier, name=identifier] + [anon `=`] > expression_list [fields: value=number, value=number]. The name list is a `variable_list` whose children carry the `name` field. There is no `name_list` node type in this grammar at all.

consequencePerPath.line 158 (extractLocalDeclaration): asks variable_declaration for 'name_list', gets null, falls back to namedChild(0). For `local c = 3` namedChild(0) is the anon `local` token, not a variable_list — so plainVariableName sees a non-identifier and returns undefined, and the declaration is SKIPPED. The `||` fallback makes this silent.
consequencePerPath.line 183 (extractAssignment): same defect on the assignment_statement path, masked there because namedChild(0) of an assignment_statement IS the variable_list.
consequencePerPath.line 208 (processCall): asks function_call for 'function', gets null, falls back to namedChild(0) which is the identifier — accidentally correct, so calls are extracted.
consequencePerPath.line 297 (extractExport): asks return_statement for 'expression_list', gets null, falls back to namedChild(0) — for `return a` that is the anon `return` token, so the export is SKIPPED.
consequencePerPath.line 393 (tableFieldNames): asks a `field` node for 'key', gets null, falls back to namedChild(0). In this grammar a table field is `field > [anon name=identifier] + [anon =] + value`, so the fallback can land on the anon name token; table field extraction is unreliable at best.

rootCause.whyItSurvived: Every one of these paths is written as `childForFieldName(X) || namedChild(0)`. The `||` is what converts 'this field does not exist' into 'quietly use whatever happens to be first', so a grammar mismatch cannot raise, cannot be logged, and cannot fail a gate. Five of the five paths still produced output, which is why a 1.000 differential on 2 hand-written fixtures did not catch it: the fixtures were authored against the same wrong expectations.
rootCause.fixShape: Replace the invented field literals with the grammar's real vocabulary (variable_list + name; the assignment_statement's own first named child; expression_list reached as a child TYPE not a field name), and make every fallback OBSERVABLE — a field literal the grammar cannot resolve must be a measured fact recorded by a gate, never a silent ||.
rootCause.gate: script/m60/verify-lua-grasped-fields.ts — 7/7 checks, 3/3 mutants planted and caught, GREEN after the fix and RED before it

CORRECTION_2026-09-26.whatIInitiallyClaimed: That the five invented fields meant five extraction paths never fired, and that fixing them would recover silently-lost declarations and exports.
CORRECTION_2026-09-26.whatMeasurementShows: The claim about the FIELDS is true and proven: name_list, function, expression_list and key resolve on no node in the pinned grammar, and each sat behind a `|| namedChild(0)`. The claim about the CONSEQUENCES was wrong, and I asserted it before measuring it.
CORRECTION_2026-09-26.measuredEvidence: Full-corpus measurement on luvit@199 files, before vs after the fix: symbols 3610 -> 3610, relationships 7257 -> 7257. BYTE-IDENTICAL. Purpose-built probes on `local solo`, `local a, b = 1, 2`, `local t = { x = 1 }` and `return name` also produced identical symbol sets before and after.
CORRECTION_2026-09-26.whyTheFallbackHappenedToWork: In this grammar a variable_declaration's first named child is EITHER a variable_list directly (`local solo` -> variable_list) OR an assignment_statement whose first named child is that variable_list (`local a, b = 1, 2` -> assignment_statement -> variable_list). The old code then iterated namedChildCount over that node, so in the second case it walked the assignment_statement's children (variable_list, expression_list) and plainVariableName rejected both — yet the symbols still came out, because a variable_list child of an assignment_statement is itself iterable by the same loop's shape on the next visit. The net effect is that the sloppy lookup and the correct one coincide on every shape in this corpus.
CORRECTION_2026-09-26.whatTheFixActuallyBought: Not one recovered symbol. It bought THREE things that are real but are not 'more output': (1) the analyzer no longer depends on a coincidence of child ordering, so a grammar revision that reorders those children cannot silently drop every local declaration in the language; (2) the `||` fallbacks that made the mismatch invisible are gone from four of the five sites, so the next grammar drift is a gate failure instead of a quiet wrong answer; (3) the gate that proves both of those now exists and can fail.
CORRECTION_2026-09-26.theLesson: I read five unreachable fields, formed a mechanism ('therefore these paths never fire'), and reported the consequence as PROVEN before running anything that would have falsified it. The honest status was SUSPECTED, the same label I correctly used for four other findings in this same ledger. A field that does not exist is a defect; a field that does not exist AND is covered by a working fallback is a latent defect, and the difference is only ever settled by a measurement.

instrument.why_standalone: The family harness script/m14/differential.ts is where M60's `diff: n/a` for lua comes from — deriveTreeEdges covers 30 languages and lua is not one. Adding the case there is the goal, but that file was observed MODIFIED IN THE WORKING TREE by a co-agent on another lane while this was written, and editing a shared file another agent is mid-edit is how lines are lost. instrument.independence: Truth is derived from the wasm parse tree. The analyzer's output is never an input to the truth side, so a dropped edge cannot drop out of both sides and read as agreement.
instrument.deliberate_non_import: The line rule is computed here from the tree rather than imported from the analyzer, so an error in the analyzer's line helper shows up as a LINE DISAGREEMENT. The family harness imports shape rules from the analyzer on purpose (#917/#919); for the line rule this instrument declines to, so the two sides can disagree about it.
instrument.oracle_bugs_found_in_itself: Two, both fixed and both recorded because the first version of this oracle reported an ANALYZER defect that was its own: (1) it attributed `function Editor:onKey` to `global` instead of to its receiver, inventing `contains global -> onKey`; (2) it used a method's FIELD name as the body scope where the tree says the FULL text, which collapsed `Editor:onKey` and a local `function onKey` into one scope and deduped two unrelated functions' calls into one edge. A declaration's name has THREE parts — label (full text, the scope), name (the field), owner (the receiver) — and conflating them is what produced both bugs.

findings.title: A method symbol is named by its FULL qualified text while its owner is also recorded, so the two identities disagree
findings.detail: extractFunction takes the symbol name from `nameNode.text`. For `function Buffer:initialize(length)` that text is `Buffer:initialize`, so the symbol is named `Buffer:initialize` AND ownerName `Buffer` AND ownerKind Class. findings.whyItMatters: M49 W2's ruling is that a member's identity is its container, not its bare name — and this satisfies neither: it is the FULL path as the name with the container duplicated alongside. A call edge targeting `initialize` can never be joined to a declaration named `Buffer:initialize`, so call-to-declaration resolution silently fails for every method in the language.

gate.mutantDiscipline: The first fourth mutant set a plain function's ownerName to 'global' and LEAKED. fix.grammar: `function Buffer:initialize()` puts a method_index_expression in the name field with the RECEIVER first and the FIELD last, so name = last named child and owner = first named child. Taking the first yields the table, not the method.
fix.threeReadings: A declaration's name has three readings and conflating them is what produced both the original defect and two bugs in the first version of the lua truth oracle: LABEL (full text, the scope a body belongs to), NAME (the field, the identity), OWNER (the receiver).

LUA_19.status: PROVEN by the truth oracle, fixed behind a permanent gate
LUA_19.title: A function nested inside another function was scoped to `global`, because `isLocal` tested for the `local` KEYWORD rather than lexical nesting
LUA_19.detail: `local function spawn(...)` at luvit/deps/childprocess.lua:72 contains `local onExit` (L74) and then `function onExit(code, signal)` (L125). The second carries no `local` keyword, so the keyword test said 'not local' and the symbol was filed with scope `global` and a `contains global -> onExit` edge. A function declared without `local` inside another function is still lexically local to it.
LUA_19.measured: 47 unexplained `contains` edges on luvit, every one a nested function. After the fix, UNEXPLAINED is 0 on luvit AND on the 400-file kong draw.
LUA_19.whyItMattered: `scope` is what a consumer reads to decide where a symbol belongs. A closure declared inside `spawn` does not belong to the file's global scope, so any consumer grouping by scope misfiled every nested function in the language.
LUA_19.whyItShowedUpOnlyInContains: Calls INSIDE a nested function were already correct, because the walk sets childFrame.callable on the way in. Only the symbol's own scope and the edge naming it used the keyword test — which is why the differential reported 47 unexplained edges and ZERO unexplained calls, a signature that pointed at identity rather than at traversal.

LUA-06.adjudication: Reproduced with two files differing only in statement order. `local A = {} / function A.new() end / A.new()` emitted `instantiates global->A`; `A.new() / local A = {} / function A.new() end` emitted NOTHING. LUA-06.fix: collectDeclaredTables runs as a PRE-PASS before the walk, so a constructor call no longer depends on where its table was declared. Both orders now emit the edge, each at its own call's line (L3 and L1 respectively).

LUA-07.adjudication: Measured directly: two locals both named `item`, one in f() and one in g(), produce DISTINCT symbols (`owner=f@L2`, `owner=g@L6`) and DISTINCT contains edges (`f->item@L2`, `g->g@L6`). LUA-08.adjudication: Measured: no symbol is ever named after a parameter list or a source snippet. `local anon = function(a,b) ... end` yields only the variable `anon`, and a nameless function as a table field yields only the table variable. resolved.adjudication: The ANALYZER was wrong. `c = nil` sits inside a closure nested in `local function adapt(c, fn, ...)` and assigns adapt's PARAMETER. The analyzer's closure frame held only the closure's own parameters, so `c` was invisible and the assignment read as a declaration — emitting a containment edge for a name with no symbol. This is LUA-21, now fixed.

The ORACLE was wrong. The oracle did not bind an anonymous function's parameters in the enclosing scope, so `srv = server()` inside a closure looked like a declaration and a genuine skip was reported as missing.

ORACLE_CORRECTIONS.defect: A name assigned in a NESTED function was treated as a declaration when it was an UPVALUE declared in an enclosing block. The oracle resolved names against the innermost scope only.
ORACLE_CORRECTIONS.correction: Names resolve up the whole SCOPE CHAIN, and a `do ... end` block does not open a scope (Lua has no block-scoped locals) — so `local paused` inside `do ... end` IS visible inside a method declared in that block.
ORACLE_CORRECTIONS.evidence: luvit/deps/codec.lua L40 declares `local paused = false` inside `do ... end`; L44 assigns it inside `function emitter:pause()`. That is an upvalue assignment, the analyzer skips it, and the analyzer is right.

Declared identity is IDENTICAL to 0.4.1 (name=lua, abiVersion=15, 22 fields, 262 states). Surface digests are identical. Per-file trees are identical on 1,510 of 1,510 files. LUA_G2_PROVENANCE_CORRECTION.theError: I compared the wired bytes against two npm REGISTRIES and concluded the bytes were unattributable. The provenance was recorded in the repository the whole time, in the lane's own manifest. I did not search it. The pin contract already has the kind for this — `local-rebuild-from-vendored-source` — and fsharp already uses it.
LUA_G2_PROVENANCE_CORRECTION.CONSEQUENCE_THE_SWAP_IS_UNNECESSARY_AND_: The wave-4 recommendation was to swap wasm/tree-sitter-lua.wasm for the 0.4.1 tarball. Swapping a documented local REBUILD for the published TARBALL changes nothing semantically — the trees are identical on 1,510 of 1,510 files — and would DISCARD the rebuild provenance the manifest records, replacing a declared fact with a different declared fact. The correct action is not a swap; it is to register lua in the pin contract with `kind: local-rebuild-from-vendored-source`, base `@tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-lua@0.4.1`, patches: none, which is a registration and not a replacement.
LUA_G2_PROVENANCE_CORRECTION.lesson: A provenance question is a question about the REPOSITORY FIRST and about the registries second. The registry sweep was real work and it did establish that the bytes are a rebuild rather than a copy — but it answered a question nobody had asked, because the answer was already written down.
